readings.title: The Lost World — excerpt: A proposal at the Chestnuts
readings.challenge: Notice where Malone, writing after the adventure, laughs at himself as he was that evening.
readings.focus: A comic refusal that gives the adventure its motive.
readings.context: The Lost World (1912) by Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes, is told by Edward Malone, a young reporter on the London Daily Gazette who joins an expedition to a South American plateau where prehistoric animals are said to survive. This is the opening of the novel; Malone is twenty-three. Bimetallism was a much-argued theory that money should rest on both gold and silver; the rupee is the money of India, then ruled by Britain; a “forlorn hope” is a desperate attack that few survive; the Freemasons are a men’s society with private meetings.
readings.contentNote: Malone states period ideas about men and women (that real love shows itself in a woman’s timidity, and once went “hand in hand” with violence) and calls Gladys’s skin “almost Oriental.” The chapter partly mocks the young man who holds these views; discuss them rather than adopt them.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “There are Heroisms all round us,” from the start to Malone jumping out of his chair; opens “Mr. Hungerton, her father, really was the most tactless person upon earth—a fluffy,…”; closes “It was my turn to jump out of my chair.”.

questions.prompt: How does Malone describe Mr. Hungerton, and what does the father contribute to the scene?
facilitatorNotes: He is “a fluffy, feathery, untidy cockatoo,” with a “monotonous chirrup” about money: a silly, self-absorbed bird of a man. His tactlessness delays the proposal, and his huffy exit for a Masonic meeting leaves the couple alone. Malone’s joking answer about being “a ruined man” also shows the young man’s own levity.
evidence: a fluffy, feathery, untidy cockatoo of a man
bounced off out of the room to dress for a Masonic meeting

questions.prompt: Why does Gladys’s frankness worry Malone? Do you trust his idea of what love looks like?
facilitatorNotes: He reads her ease as friendship, not love: he expects love to show as timidity, “the averted eye.” Readers may find the idea old-fashioned or self-serving, since it lets him explain away her frankness. Malone, writing it down later, half-admits this, calling the feeling “primitive and bestial.”
evidence: My instincts are all against a woman being too frank and at her ease with me.
How primitive and bestial it looks when you put it down in black and white!

questions.prompt: Gladys sees the proposal coming before he speaks. How does she stay in control of the conversation?
facilitatorNotes: She names it first (“a presentiment”), argues for friendship, stands up when he moves closer, and sets the terms for him to sit and talk. He pleads; she judges. A reader may still feel she is kind as well as firm.
evidence: I have a presentiment that you are going to propose, Ned.
She had sprung from her chair as she saw signs that I proposed to demonstrate some of my wants.

questions.prompt: Find a moment where the narrator makes his own declaration ridiculous. Why might an adventure story open with a comic failure?
facilitatorNotes: The station-master who “trotted” in, and the cut-off “I want——”, deflate his romance. Opening with failure makes Malone likeable and modest and gives him something to prove; the last line, “somebody else,” leaves a question that the next part of the chapter answers.
evidence: I can't imagine how that official came into the matter, but in he trotted and set us both laughing.
I'm in love with somebody else

readings.title: The Lost World — excerpt: “There are heroisms all round us”
readings.challenge: Separate what Gladys says she wants from what her examples reveal about her.
readings.focus: An ideal of heroism that the novel will test, and a doubt the narrator raises and puts aside.
readings.context: Recap: Malone, a young reporter, has proposed to Gladys Hungerton; she refused him and said she loves “somebody else.” The explorers Richard Burton and Henry Morton Stanley were famous in Victorian Britain, and both of their wives published books about them. Robert Clive began as a clerk for the East India Company and led the battles that began British rule in India. Teetotal means never drinking alcohol; an aeronaut is a balloonist; a Theosophist belongs to a mystical religious movement; the “Superman” is the philosopher Nietzsche’s ideal man, long before the comic-book hero. Choke-damp is the suffocating gas left in a coal mine after an explosion; “copy” is material for a newspaper; “bucking” is boasting. The 1912 printing reads “adopt himself” where “adapt” is meant; the text keeps it as printed.
readings.contentNote: Clive’s conquest of India is held up as heroism, a view of empire common in Britain in 1912.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “There are Heroisms all round us,” from Gladys’s “ideal” to the end of the chapter; opens “"It's nobody in particular," she explained, laughing at the expression of my face, "only…”; closes “…come to middle age, but never to ardent three-and-twenty in the fever of his first love.”.

questions.prompt: Gladys says it is “never a man” she would love. What would she love instead, and why does she want it?
facilitatorNotes: The glories he has won, because they would be “reflected upon me.” Her examples are wives admired for their husbands’ fame. Some readers find her honest about wanting greatness; others find the wish selfish. The text supports both.
evidence: It is never a man that I should love, but always the glories he had won, for they would be reflected upon me.

questions.prompt: Malone has already gone down a mine after an explosion. Why does that not satisfy Gladys?
facilitatorNotes: He did it to “write good copy,” not for the glory of it, and he never boasted. She calls this “a prosaic motive,” although she is glad he went. The irony is that real courage, done quietly for work, does not fit her romantic ideal.
evidence: There was nothing worth bucking about.
What a prosaic motive!

questions.prompt: What does Gladys mean by “heroisms all round us waiting to be done”? How does Malone take up the idea?
facilitatorNotes: She means that great deeds are available to anyone who goes looking, like the balloonist who started in a gale. Malone seizes it at once (“Give me a chance”) and leaves determined to find a deed worthy of her. The phrase gives the chapter its title and the whole book its motive.
evidence: There are heroisms all round us waiting to be done.
not another day should elapse before I should find some deed which was worthy of my lady

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph Malone asks, “Was it hardness, was it selfishness, that she should ask me to risk my life for her own glorification?” How does he answer, and who is really asking?
facilitatorNotes: Malone asks it as he writes, after the adventure; at twenty-three, on that evening, he could not have. The question plants a doubt that the reader can carry through the adventure, while the answer excuses the young man’s blindness rather than Gladys.
evidence: Such thoughts may come to middle age, but never to ardent three-and-twenty in the fever of his first love.

readings.title: The Lost World — excerpt: A letter under false colours
readings.challenge: Sort what Tarp Henry knows from what he has only heard, and count the untruths in Malone’s letter.
readings.focus: Reputation, gossip and a reporter’s trick.
readings.context: The Lost World (1912) by Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes, is told by Edward Malone, a young reporter on the London Daily Gazette who joins an expedition to a South American plateau where prehistoric animals are said to survive. Malone’s editor has suggested he try to interview Professor Challenger, a zoologist famous for attacking reporters, and handed him a short record of Challenger’s career. Malone goes to his club to ask about him. Nature is a scientific journal; Reuter’s is a news agency; “bowdlerized” means cleaned of rude words; conversaziones are evening gatherings for learned talk. August Weismann (spelled Weissmann here) was a German biologist whose theory of heredity divided scientists after Darwin; an “id” was his word for a unit of hereditary material.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Try your Luck with Professor Challenger,” from Malone’s arrival at the club to the end of the chapter; opens “I entered the club. It was just after eleven, and the big room was fairly full, though…”; closes “…with him. Perhaps it would be best for you if you never heard from the fellow at all."”.

questions.prompt: What does Tarp Henry tell Malone about Challenger? Which parts are facts he knows and which are reports or opinion?
facilitatorNotes: He calls Challenger’s South American story “rank nonsense,” says he faked photographs and quarrelled in Vienna, and admits he knows only what he has “heard.” Most of it is reputation and gossip, from a man who says he is “too detached to talk scandal” and then talks it. The faked photographs, in particular, are reported, not shown.
evidence: He had gone the length of faking some photographs over the South American business.
I'm too detached to talk scandal

questions.prompt: How does the exchange between Wadley and Challenger work as a joke? What does it show about Challenger?
facilitatorNotes: Challenger copies the polite formula of the invitation word for word and turns its ending into an insult. He uses the forms of courtesy to be rude, which is cleverer and more wounding than plain abuse.
evidence: would take it as a personal favour if he would go to the devil

questions.prompt: Why does Tarp Henry murmur “You infernal liar!”? List the untruths in Malone’s letter.
facilitatorNotes: Malone is no “humble student” who has always followed the debate; he has not read the address, which he admits he cannot follow, and has picked one “meaty” sentence he only vaguely understands. He has no “certain suggestions” to discuss. The letter is a trick to get through the door.
evidence: As a humble student of Nature, I have always taken the most profound interest
I seem in a vague way almost to understand it.

questions.prompt: “If he is a sportsman he will be tickled.” Is Malone’s plan clever, dishonest or foolish? Use the last paragraph in your answer.
facilitatorNotes: He treats the deception as a game and hopes for a sporting reaction or even a confession. Tarp Henry expects violence (“Chain mail, or an American football suit”). Readers may admire the nerve, object to the lying, or see a newspaper’s habits at work; the warning prepares the next chapter.
evidence: I may even go the length of open confession.
Chain mail, or an American football suit—that's what you'll want.

readings.title: The Lost World — excerpt: Gladys Potts and the cigar-box
readings.challenge: Follow a rapid change of tone, from bitterness to comedy to a quiet ending.
readings.focus: How the novel answers the question its first chapter asked.
readings.context: The Lost World (1912) by Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes, is told by Edward Malone, a young reporter on the London Daily Gazette who joins an expedition to a South American plateau where prehistoric animals are said to survive. Malone went to South America to do something heroic for Gladys Hungerton, who had told him she could love only a man of great deeds; on the plateau he named a lake after her. Now the travellers are back in London, where crowds carried them through the streets after Challenger showed a living pterodactyl to a packed hall. Para (Pará) is a Brazilian port; Streatham is a London suburb; a solicitor’s clerk works in a lawyer’s office; the “electric push” is a bell-button for calling a servant; a spud is a small digging tool; De Beers ran the great diamond mine at Kimberley in South Africa; Spink’s was a London dealer. The 1912 printing reads “Gladys,!” and “its facts”; both are kept as printed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “A Procession! A Procession!”, from “And Gladys” to the end of the novel; opens “And Gladys—oh, my Gladys!—Gladys of the mystic lake, now to be re-named the Central, for…”; closes “Lord Roxton said nothing, but a brown hand was stretched out to me across the table.”.

questions.prompt: The first paragraph is a string of questions about Gladys. What is Malone suggesting, and what does his last question admit?
facilitatorNotes: He suggests that he always saw “selfishness” and “fickleness” in her, behind her beauty. Then he asks whether this is only “the vain wisdom which comes after the event”: hindsight, rewriting the past to protect his pride. A careful reader might believe him half.
evidence: discern the twin shadows of selfishness and of fickleness
Or are these thoughts the vain wisdom which comes after the event?

questions.prompt: How does Doyle make the meeting with Gladys and her husband comic rather than tragic?
facilitatorNotes: The grand name becomes “Gladys Potts”; the husband is “coiled up” in Malone’s old chair; the rivals bob and grin; Malone manages “Oh, yes” and “It is quite clear.” Malone himself calls it absurd. The comedy lets him, and the reader, laugh at the romance of Chapter I.
evidence: I am Gladys Potts.
We bobbed and grinned in front of each other.

questions.prompt: Malone asks whether the husband has “searched for hidden treasure, or discovered a pole.” Why is “I am a solicitor's clerk” the perfect answer?
facilitatorNotes: Gladys wanted a hero and married the most ordinary of men, which makes her speeches about great deeds look empty. (In Chapter I Malone cited Clive as “just a clerk” who conquered India; this clerk has conquered only Gladys.) The answer also mocks Malone for expecting romance to explain everything.
evidence: Where is the glamour of romance? How did you get it?
I am a solicitor's clerk

questions.prompt: At the end Malone chooses to go with Lord John rather than marry. Has he become the man Gladys wanted? What has changed in what he wants?
facilitatorNotes: He has done great deeds, but no longer for a woman’s admiration; he wants the adventure and the comradeship themselves. Lord John’s silent handshake seals a friendship that has replaced the courtship. Some readers will see growth; others, a young man running from disappointment.
evidence: I think, if you will have me, that I would rather go with you.
Lord Roxton said nothing, but a brown hand was stretched out to me across the table.
